The Richmond City Council has accepted the need and desirability of the Randolph Conservation and Redevelopment Program as is evident in the Community Renewal Program and in the five (5) year Capital Improvement Program. Official local approval by the City Council is expected in February, 1973. City Departments involved are prepared to support the project with necessary public works and community facilities improvements and other official agencies such as the State Water Control Board and Richmond Metropolitan Authority are cooperating to make the project successful.
C. Aesthetic Environment:
1. Aesthetics of the Area:
The existing area is composed of visual and environmental a. contrasts. As previously discussed, the project appears to be comprised of three sub-areas, each with a character and intrinsic esthetic value unique to itself, but each area is environmentally dependent on the others. The Randolph Project Area has distinct natural boundaries on three sides; Byrd Park on the west, Mount Calvary and Riverview Cemeteries on the south, and Hollywood Cemetery on the east. These are historic and established areas that will change very little. They offer those areas of the Randolph project landscaped and aesthetically pleasing visual open space, unique in the urban environment. The fourth side, the northern boundary, will become positively defined with the construction of the proposed Downtown Expressway. The Randolph project area will become distinct, and in some ways, a blend of suburban and urban characteristics. Each of the sub-areas will become more functionally dependent on the others, each will become more vulnerable to the others. The tree lined streets and sound brick homes found in the western edge of Randolph, and the individual frame homes are on larger lots, are modest and sound, and are in juxtaposition with significant blight, decay, and crowded and hazardous conditions found in the northeast section of the project. Visually the Randolph project is esthetically pleasing. Realistically, the area is under very strong and significant pressure from blight, structural obsolescence, and inequality of open space. A majority of the open space east of Meadow Street is adjacent areas of low density. These visual and environmental contrasts have been effectively dealt with in the proposed Redevelopment and Conservation Plan.
